garlic.shortDescription: Garlic is a plant with a distinctive aroma and flavour that comes from its natural sulfur compounds, particularly allicin. Garlic also contains fructans, carbohydrates that can serve as a food source for certain gut microorganisms, while its sulfur compounds have been studied for their relationship with oxidative balance and the body's processes for handling foreign substances.
garlic.fullDescription:
Garlic (Allium sativum L.) has a history of use as both a food and an herb in many cultures around the world. What makes garlic unique is not only its pungent smell and hot, spicy taste, but also the chemical reaction that takes place when a garlic clove is crushed, chopped or sliced: the enzyme alliinase reacts with alliin to form allicin, which can then be converted into other sulfur compounds.

Another interesting component of garlic is fructans, carbohydrates that human digestive enzymes cannot break down efficiently. As a result, they can travel through the digestive tract to the large intestine and serve as a food source for certain microorganisms. Microbial fermentation of fructans also leads to the production of short-chain fatty acids, which are associated with the intestinal environment and the function of the cells lining the gut.

From a biochemical perspective, the sulfur compounds in garlic, such as diallyl disulfide (DADS), diallyl trisulfide (DATS) and S-allyl cysteine (SAC), have also been studied for their relationship with antioxidant mechanisms, liver enzyme activity and the body's processes for transforming foreign substances.
garlic.howItWorks:
Garlic and how it works in the body
1. Prebiotic properties and gut microorganisms
The human gut is home to a wide variety of microorganisms that play a role in digestion, metabolism and the immune system. The fructans found in garlic can serve as a food source for certain groups of microorganisms, such as Bifidobacterium, although the response to garlic may vary according to the composition of each individual's gut microbiota.
2. Production of short-chain fatty acids and the intestinal environment
When microorganisms in the large intestine use fructans through fermentation, short-chain fatty acids (SCFAs) such as acetate, propionate and butyrate are produced. Butyrate in particular is an important energy source for the cells lining the large intestine. This process is part of the relationship between diet, microorganisms and the function of the digestive system.
3. The body's processes for handling foreign substances
The liver plays an important role in transforming various substances through biochemical processes, so that the body can handle and eliminate certain substances. Sulfur compounds in garlic, such as DADS and DATS, have been studied for their relationship with the Nrf2 signalling pathway and the enzyme glutathione S-transferase (GST), which are involved in the body's processes for transforming foreign substances.
4. Oxidative balance and blood vessel health
The sulfur compounds in garlic have also been studied for their relationship with the body's natural antioxidant system, the function of the cells lining the blood vessels and lipid metabolism, another dimension of research into the biological properties of garlic beyond the digestive system.
garlic.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of garlic
Garlic can be consumed in many forms, from an everyday cooking ingredient to extracts in dietary supplements. The method of preparation and processing affects its aroma, flavour and the composition of its key compounds.
Fresh garlic: commonly eaten raw or used in cooking; it contains both fructans and the precursors that can be converted into allicin when crushed or sliced.
Cooked garlic: commonly stir-fried, boiled, baked or grilled; heat can affect the activity of the enzyme alliinase and the amount of allicin.
Garlic powder: made from garlic that has been dried and finely ground; commonly used as a seasoning and as an ingredient in dietary supplements.
Garlic oil: distilled types usually contain oil-soluble sulfur compounds such as DADS and DATS, but are not a source of fructans in the way fresh garlic is.
Aged garlic extract: goes through an ageing process that changes its chemical composition, with key compounds such as S-allyl cysteine (SAC).
Black garlic: processed under controlled temperature and humidity; it has a soft texture, a sweet-sour taste and a less pungent smell than fresh garlic.
garlic.scientificEvidence:
1. Garlic and gut microbiota composition
A 2024 study examined the effects of garlic on gut microorganisms using a model in which microorganisms from human faecal samples were cultured, comparing the responses of microbial communities with different compositions.
The study found that garlic affected the composition and diversity of the microorganisms differently depending on the characteristics of the original microbial community, and also observed an increase in bacteria of the Bifidobacterium group and promotion of the growth of Bifidobacterium adolescentis in culture.
However, this study was a laboratory experiment, not a trial in which people ate garlic directly, so further clinical studies are still needed.
2. Garlic and intestinal transit time
A randomised, double-blind, controlled study from 2023, published in the journal Phytotherapy Research, studied 90 people with metabolic syndrome over 3 months, comparing a group given garlic powder with a group given a placebo.
The study reported results on intestinal transit time and metabolic markers, which provides interesting data on the relationship between garlic and the function of the digestive system.
However, the study was conducted in a specific population, so its results cannot yet be used to confirm that garlic helps improve bowel movements in the general population.
3. Sulfur compounds and enzymes involved in handling foreign substances
A 2019 study examined alliin and sulfur compounds from garlic, assessing their relationship with glutathione levels, the activity of the enzymes glutathione S-transferase (GST) and glutathione peroxidase (GPx), and the Nrf2 signalling pathway.
Results from animal and cell experiments showed changes in markers related to the antioxidant system and the liver's processes for handling foreign substances, improving understanding of the biochemical mechanisms of sulfur compounds.
However, these findings are not yet evidence confirming effectiveness in detoxifying or cleansing the intestines in humans.
*This information is provided for educational purposes about garlic and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
garlic.safetyInformation:
Garlic is high in fructans and is classified as a high-FODMAP food, which may cause gas, bloating or abdominal pain in people who are sensitive to this group of carbohydrates, especially those with irritable bowel syndrome (IBS).
Eating raw garlic or large amounts of garlic may cause nausea, stomach discomfort, bad breath and body odour.
Garlic supplements may increase the risk of bleeding. People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should consult a doctor before use.
People who are scheduled for surgery should inform their doctor if they are taking dietary supplements containing garlic.
Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a doctor before taking garlic in dietary supplement form.
People with a history of garlic allergy should avoid products containing garlic.
keyFunctions: Contains fructans, which can serve as a food source for certain gut microorganisms
Contains allicin and sulfur compounds that have been studied for their interactions with microorganisms in the digestive tract
Has been studied for its relationship with intestinal transit time
Contains natural compounds that have been studied for their antioxidant properties
Contains sulfur compounds that have been studied for their relationship with enzymes in the body's processes for handling foreign substances

green-tea.shortDescription: Green tea is a beverage familiar to many people. It contains key compounds such as catechins and EGCG, which are natural antioxidants. These compounds are currently attracting researchers' interest in relation to energy metabolism, blood vessel function and the protection of cells from damage caused by free radicals.
green-tea.fullDescription:
Green tea, black tea and oolong tea may differ in colour, aroma and flavour so much that they seem like different kinds of tea, but in fact all three can be produced from the same plant, Camellia sinensis. The key difference lies in how the tea leaves are processed: green tea is heated to inhibit the enzymes that cause the compounds in the leaves to oxidise, which helps preserve more of the catechins compared with fully oxidised teas.

One of the compounds attracting the most interest is EGCG (epigallocatechin gallate), a catechin that belongs to the polyphenol group. Researchers study the association of EGCG with cell function, metabolism and the response to oxidative stress.

Green tea also contains other catechins, such as epicatechin (EC), epicatechin gallate (ECG) and epigallocatechin (EGC), as well as caffeine and the amino acid L-theanine, components that contribute to the distinctive character of tea.
green-tea.howItWorks:
Green tea and how it works in the body
1. Association with the body's energy use
Catechins, particularly EGCG, and the caffeine in green tea have been studied in relation to the body's energy use, including heat production (thermogenesis) and the use of fat as a main energy source.
2. The role of EGCG in oxidative stress
EGCG has a chemical structure that can interact with free radicals in laboratory experiments, and it has been studied in relation to the systems that regulate the response to oxidative stress within cells.
3. Association with blood vessel function
The polyphenols in green tea have been studied in relation to the function of the cells lining the blood vessel walls, which play a role in regulating the dilation and constriction of blood vessels as well as the response to signalling molecules in the body.
green-tea.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of green tea
Green tea is a herbal plant and beverage that is popular around the world. It is consumed in many different forms, from an everyday drink to standardised extracts in the health industry, as follows:
• Dried green tea leaves and brewed tea: fresh green tea leaves are heated quickly, by roasting or steaming, to inhibit the enzymes and prevent fermentation, and are then dried. They are brewed with hot water as a drink, giving a natural flavour and aroma.
• Matcha powder: green tea leaves that are shaded before harvest are dried and ground with a stone mill into a fine powder. The whole leaf is drunk without straining, or the powder is used as an ingredient in food and desserts.
• Ready-to-drink green tea beverages: green tea in bottles or cans, available both as natural unsweetened versions and flavoured versions.
• Green tea extract: green tea leaves go through an extraction process to standardise the content of key polyphenols, especially EGCG, as well as L-theanine. It is commonly used in dietary supplements in capsule or tablet form.
green-tea.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on weight control and metabolism
A systematic review by Jurgens et al. (2012), published in the Cochrane Database of Systematic Reviews, evaluated randomised trials of green tea extract for weight loss and weight maintenance.
The analysis found that green tea use in overweight or obese adults had a relatively small effect on weight loss, and no clearly clinically significant outcomes were found overall.
Although catechins and caffeine have been studied in relation to the body's energy use, the evidence is not yet sufficient to conclude that green tea extract can effectively help with weight loss.
2. Studies on blood vessel function
A Cochrane review by Hartley et al. (2013) evaluated trials of green and black tea on cardiovascular risk factors and found that some studies reported changes in blood lipid levels and blood pressure.
However, most of the trials were relatively short and used different products, so long-term effects on the development of cardiovascular disease cannot yet be confirmed.
3. Studies on oxidative stress
EGCG and catechins have been widely studied for their antioxidant properties, particularly in cell and animal experiments, which have found associations with the processes involved in responding to oxidative stress.
However, results in humans are not entirely consistent, because catechins have limited absorption and are transformed within the body, so it cannot yet be confirmed that taking green tea extract helps prevent cell degeneration or any disease.
This information is provided for educational purposes about green tea and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
green-tea.safetyInformation:
• The caffeine in green tea may cause insomnia, palpitations, restlessness or stomach discomfort in people who are sensitive to caffeine.
• Concentrated green tea extracts, especially formulas with high amounts of EGCG, may carry a risk of liver injury, although this is uncommon.
• People with liver disease or a history of liver abnormalities should consult a doctor before using green tea extract.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should take into account their total caffeine intake from food and beverages, and avoid using concentrated extracts without advice from a healthcare professional.
• Drinking tea close to mealtimes may reduce the absorption of non-heme iron from certain foods, especially in people at risk of iron deficiency.
keyFunctions: Contains catechins and EGCG, compounds that have been studied in relation to oxidative stress
Has been researched in relation to the body's energy use and metabolism
Has been clinically studied in relation to markers of weight and body composition
Contains key compounds that have been studied in relation to blood vessel function

fish-oil-powder.shortDescription: Fish oil is a source of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA and DHA, which play an important role in the structure and function of cells, as well as in the cardiovascular system, the brain and the eyes.
fish-oil-powder.fullDescription:
Fish oil is oil obtained from the tissues of fish, especially oily fish such as salmon, sardines and mackerel. Its key feature is that it is a source of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly eicosapentaenoic acid (EPA) and docosahexaenoic acid (DHA), fatty acids involved in the structure of cell membranes and the normal functioning of the body.

Although the terms fish oil and omega-3 are often mentioned together, they do not mean exactly the same thing. Omega-3 is a group of fatty acids found in many food sources, while fish oil is one source of EPA and DHA. DHA is found as an important component of brain cells and the retina, while EPA is involved in the production of signalling molecules in the body, particularly processes related to the inflammatory response.

What is the difference between fish oil and omega-3?

Many people may think that fish oil and omega-3 are the same thing, but in fact fish oil is a source of omega-3 fatty acids, while omega-3 is a group of fatty acids found in both fish-based and plant-based foods, with different sources and different roles in the body, as follows:

| Omega-3 fatty acid | Sources and properties |
| EPA | Found in fish and fish oil; involved in the production of signalling molecules in the body |
| DHA | Found in fish and fish oil; an important component of the brain and retina |
| ALA | Found in flaxseed, chia seeds and some vegetable oils; the body can convert it into EPA and DHA in limited amounts |
fish-oil-powder.howItWorks:
Fish oil and how it works in the body
1. The cardiovascular system
Fish oil is a source of EPA and DHA, which play a role in the functioning of the cardiovascular system. Both fatty acids can become components of cell membranes and are involved in the production of signalling molecules in the body. The effects of EPA and DHA on blood triglyceride levels have also been studied.
2. The nervous system and vision
DHA is a fatty acid found in high amounts in the membranes of nerve cells and the retina, especially in the photoreceptor cells, and is important for signalling and the normal functioning of the visual system.
3. Response to inflammatory processes
EPA and DHA from fish oil can be used as precursors for producing compounds involved in the body's natural processes for regulating and resolving inflammation, such as resolvins and protectins. The role of these fatty acids has therefore been studied in the context of cell function and the inflammatory response.
fish-oil-powder.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of fish oil
• Liquid fish oil: oil extracted from fish and processed according to specified standards.
• Fish oil capsules: fish oil filled into capsules for convenient consumption.
• Fish oil powder: fish oil processed into a powder, often using technology that encapsulates the oil particles.
• Foods containing omega-3: such as salmon, sardines and mackerel, which are natural sources of EPA and DHA.
fish-oil-powder.scientificEvidence:
1. EPA and DHA and the cardiovascular system
Information from the National Institutes of Health (NIH) explains that EPA and DHA play an important role in the functioning of the cardiovascular system, and there is clinical research on their effects on triglyceride levels.
However, evidence on reducing the risk of cardiovascular disease with omega-3 supplements varies according to the formulation, dose and population studied.
2. DHA and the brain and eyes
DHA is an important component of the cell membranes of the brain and retina and plays a role in the structure and function of these cells. Clinical research is still studying the relationship between DHA intake and cognitive function and eye health.
However, it cannot yet be concluded that fish oil supplementation helps improve brain function or prevent vision degeneration in the general population.
3. EPA and DHA and inflammatory processes
Biochemical studies have found that EPA and DHA are precursors of signalling molecules involved in the body's natural regulation and resolution of inflammation. Although these mechanisms continue to be studied, clinical trial results vary according to health status and the form of fatty acid intake.
This information is provided for educational purposes about fish oil and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
fish-oil-powder.safetyInformation:
• Taking fish oil may cause fishy burps, nausea, stomach discomfort or diarrhoea in some people.
• People who are allergic to seafish or fish oil should avoid products containing these ingredients.
• People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should consult a doctor before using fish oil products, especially in high doses.
• People with blood clotting disorders or who are scheduled for surgery should inform their doctor about the products they are taking.
• High intakes of omega-3 may increase the risk of atrial fibrillation in some populations.
keyFunctions: A source of omega-3 fatty acids, particularly EPA and DHA
EPA and DHA contribute to the normal function of the heart
DHA is an important component of the cell membranes of the brain and retina
Omega-3 fatty acids are involved in the structure and function of cell membranes
EPA and DHA are precursors of certain signalling molecules involved in inflammatory processes

korean-ginseng.shortDescription: Korean ginseng is an herb with a long history of use in Asia, particularly its root, which contains key compounds known as ginsenosides. It is currently attracting interest in relation to energy and fatigue, immune system function and men's health.
korean-ginseng.fullDescription:
When it comes to herbs renowned for strength and vitality, Korean ginseng is probably one of the first names many people think of. This herb has a long history of use in traditional Asian remedies and continues to attract interest in the scientific community, particularly in the study of the natural compounds hidden within the ginseng root.

Korean ginseng has the scientific name Panax ginseng C.A.Mey. and is a plant in the Araliaceae family. The part most commonly used is the root, which contains several groups of key compounds, particularly ginsenosides, or saponins, which researchers study in relation to cell function, the response to physical stress, immune system function and men's sexual health.

Another interesting point is that red ginseng and white ginseng are not different varieties of ginseng but come from the same plant. White ginseng is usually simply dried, while red ginseng is steamed before drying. These processes may change the proportions of ginsenosides, giving each form of ginseng a different chemical composition.
korean-ginseng.howItWorks:
Korean ginseng and how it works in the body
1. Association with the response to fatigue
Some ginsenosides have been studied in relation to cellular energy use and the response to physical stress, and may be associated with cellular pathways that help maintain the balance between energy use and energy production.
2. Role in immune system function
Korean ginseng contains ginsenosides and polysaccharides that have been studied in relation to the function of immune cells, and may interact with signalling processes involved in the body's responses.
3. Association with blood vessel function
Some ginsenosides have been studied in relation to the function of blood vessel walls and the production of nitric oxide, a compound involved in the relaxation of blood vessels. This mechanism is one of the topics researchers are interested in with regard to men's health.
korean-ginseng.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of Korean ginseng
Korean ginseng is an herb with a long history of consumption, and it is processed and consumed in a variety of forms, as follows:
• Fresh ginseng and foods containing ginseng: fresh ginseng root that has not been dried, commonly used in Korean cooking, for example in ginseng chicken soup, or sliced and preserved in honey to be eaten.
• Dried ginseng and ginseng tea: ginseng root that has been dried naturally (white ginseng) or steamed with heat before drying (red ginseng), cut into slices to be boiled as a drink, or ground into a powder to be brewed as an everyday tea.
• Concentrated ginseng extract drinks: ginseng extract in concentrated liquid form, packed in ready-to-drink sachets or bottles, a popular form for everyday use.
• Standardised Korean ginseng extract: ginseng root (especially red ginseng) goes through an extraction process to standardise the content of the key compounds, ginsenosides, to a set percentage concentration. It is commonly filled into dietary supplement capsules for convenient intake and a consistent amount of key compounds.
korean-ginseng.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on fatigue
An analysis by Bach et al. (2016) pooled the results of randomised trials on the use of ginseng for fatigue and physical performance, and found that ginseng may help reduce fatigue scores in some groups of participants. However, the results for physical performance remain unclear, and the studies analysed used different types of ginseng and product forms.
2. Studies on the immune system
There have been clinical trials of Korean ginseng and red ginseng on the immune response, with some studies reporting changes in immune markers or outcomes related to respiratory infections. However, the evidence is still limited by sample size, differences between products and study quality.
3. Studies on men's sexual health
A Cochrane review by Lee et al. (2021) evaluated randomised trials on the use of ginseng for erectile dysfunction and found that ginseng may have only a small effect, or no clinically significant effect, on erectile function compared with placebo, although some participants reported improved outcomes in their ability to have sexual intercourse.
This information is provided for educational purposes about Korean ginseng and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
korean-ginseng.safetyInformation:
• Korean ginseng may cause insomnia, especially in people who are sensitive to the extract or who take it close to bedtime. Some people may experience headaches, stomach discomfort or other adverse effects.
• People with underlying medical conditions or who use immunosuppressants, as well as those taking anticoagulants, should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• People taking blood-sugar-lowering medicines should be cautious, as ginseng may affect blood sugar levels and increase the risk when used together with certain medicines.
• Pregnant women, breastfeeding women and children should avoid using concentrated ginseng extracts without advice from a healthcare professional.
keyFunctions: Contains ginsenosides, key compounds that have been studied in relation to cell function
Has been clinically studied in relation to fatigue and feelings of tiredness
Contains compounds that have been studied in relation to the immune response
Has been researched in relation to blood vessel function and men's sexual health

ginger.shortDescription: Ginger is an herbal plant that has long been used both in food and in traditional knowledge. It contains key compounds known as gingerols and shogaols, which contribute to its distinctive hot, spicy taste. Ginger is currently attracting research interest in relation to the digestive system and gastric motility.
ginger.fullDescription:
Ginger is a kitchen herb that many people know for its aroma and hot, spicy taste, but behind this distinctive flavour lies something that has caught scientists' attention, particularly gingerols and shogaols, key compounds that have been studied in relation to the digestive system and the body's functions.

Ginger has the scientific name Zingiber officinale Roscoe and belongs to the Zingiberaceae family. The part most commonly used is the underground rhizome, which can be consumed fresh, dried or processed, and each form may have a different composition of key compounds.

Interestingly, fresh ginger usually contains 6-gingerol as a key component, while drying or heating can convert some gingerols into shogaols. This difference is one reason why researchers are interested in the different forms of ginger, particularly in studying their biological properties and their association with the function of the digestive tract.
ginger.howItWorks:
Ginger and how it works in the body
1. Gastric motility
Some compounds in ginger have been studied in relation to the function of smooth muscle in the digestive tract, including the process of moving food from the stomach to the small intestine, known as gastric emptying.
2. Digestive tract responses
Gingerols and shogaols have been studied in relation to signalling through certain receptors in the digestive tract and nervous system, including pathways involving the neurotransmitter serotonin.
3. Cellular response processes
Laboratory studies have found that gingerols and shogaols can interact with certain cellular signalling pathways involved in oxidative stress and the inflammatory response.
ginger.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of ginger
Ginger is an herb that can be consumed in many forms, from a fresh cooking ingredient to a wide range of processed health extracts.
• Fresh ginger: the fresh rhizome is sliced, shredded or juiced for use as a spice in cooking and in drinks, providing a hot, spicy taste and the aroma of its natural essential oils.
• Ginger tea and instant ginger powder: dried ginger is broken into pieces for brewing as tea, or made into a ready-to-mix drink powder, suitable for drinking to relax and for general health care.
• Pickled ginger: young ginger is pickled in vinegar and sugar and is commonly eaten as a side dish in Asian cuisine to cleanse the palate and complement the flavour of food.
• Ginger extract: ginger goes through an extraction process to standardise the content of key compounds, such as gingerols and shogaols, to consistent proportions. It is commonly filled into dietary supplements in capsule or tablet form for convenient intake.
ginger.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on gastric motility
Reviews of clinical evidence on ginger have found that some studies report effects on the time it takes for food to leave the stomach, but the results are not consistent across all trials, and there are limitations in the number of participants, product forms and methods of measurement. It therefore cannot yet be clearly concluded that all types of ginger help the digestive system work better.
2. Clinical evidence on nausea
Several systematic reviews have found that some forms of ginger may help reduce the severity of nausea in pregnant women. However, the quality of the evidence varies, and study results on nausea from travel, surgery or chemotherapy are not entirely consistent, so these results should not be used to claim the effectiveness of every ginger extract formula.
3. Studies on the inflammatory response
Reviews pooling clinical studies have found changes in certain markers related to oxidative stress and inflammation, such as C-reactive protein (CRP) and malondialdehyde (MDA). However, the level of certainty of the evidence varies and is not yet sufficient to draw conclusions about preventing or treating disease.
This information is provided for educational purposes about ginger and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
ginger.safetyInformation:
• Taking ginger or ginger extract may cause heartburn, stomach discomfort, diarrhoea or irritation of the mouth and throat in some people.
• People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should consult a doctor before using ginger extract, as there are concerns about herb-drug interactions.
• People with gallstones or bile duct disease should consult a doctor before using ginger extract, especially high-concentration products.
• Pregnant and breastfeeding women should consult a healthcare professional before using ginger in supplement form, even though the use of ginger in pregnant women has been studied.
keyFunctions: Contains key compounds known as gingerols and shogaols, which have antioxidant properties
Is associated with gastric motility and the functioning of the digestive system
Contains key compounds that have been studied in relation to the response to inflammatory processes at the cellular level
Contains essential oil components that give it its characteristic aroma and compounds that give it its hot, spicy taste

ginkgo-biloba.shortDescription: Ginkgo biloba leaf is part of a plant with a long history of use. Ginkgo leaf extract contains key compounds, namely flavonoids and terpene lactones, which are attracting interest in studies on memory, brain function and blood circulation.
ginkgo-biloba.fullDescription:
Ginkgo biloba leaf is one of the herbal plants attracting a great deal of interest in studies on memory, brain function and blood circulation, particularly among older adults and people interested in looking after their brain health as they age. Although ginkgo leaf has a long history of use, what makes this plant of interest today is the natural compounds found in its leaves, which scientists study to understand how they work in the body.

The key compounds in ginkgo leaf are flavonoids and terpene lactones, which have been studied for their antioxidant properties as well as mechanisms related to nerve cells and blood vessels. These compounds are therefore a key reason why ginkgo leaf continues to be studied today in relation to brain health and blood circulation.

What are the key compounds in ginkgo leaf?

1. Flavonoids

A group of plant compounds that have shown antioxidant properties in laboratory experiments. Ginkgo leaf extract commonly contains derivatives of quercetin, kaempferol and isorhamnetin.

2. Terpene lactones

These include ginkgolides and bilobalide, compounds found specifically in ginkgo that have been studied in relation to mechanisms involving the nervous system and platelet function. However, the results of these mechanistic studies cannot yet be used to directly confirm clinical benefits.
ginkgo-biloba.howItWorks:
Ginkgo leaf and how it works in the body
1. Role in blood circulation
Some compounds in ginkgo leaf have been studied in relation to blood vessel function and blood circulation, particularly ginkgolides, which affect signalling molecules involved in platelet aggregation.
2. Protecting cells from oxidative stress
Ginkgo leaf contains flavonoids, which have shown antioxidant properties in laboratory studies and are associated with reducing the reactions of free radicals that may affect cell components.
3. Association with the function of the nervous system and brain
The key compounds in ginkgo leaf have been studied in relation to nerve cell function, including signalling between cells and the response of cells to stress.
ginkgo-biloba.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of ginkgo leaf
Because fresh ginkgo leaves naturally contain ginkgolic acid, which must be removed and strictly controlled according to safety standards, they are not usually eaten fresh but are processed through extraction instead. The main forms are as follows:
• Standardised extract in dietary supplements: in capsule form, the most popular form and the one supported by the most research. It goes through an extraction process to standardise the proportions of key compounds to appropriate levels with high purity.
• Ginkgo leaf herbal tea: ginkgo leaves that have been dried and processed for safety are ground for brewing as a drink.
• Liquid extract: key compounds are extracted in concentrated liquid form for use as an ingredient in health formulas.
ginkgo-biloba.scientificEvidence:
• Memory and brain function: ginkgo leaf extract has been studied in relation to memory and thinking ability, but there is no clear evidence that it helps improve memory or concentration in healthy people.
• Brain health in older adults: a large study in more than 3,000 older adults did not find that ginkgo leaf extract helped reduce the risk of dementia or slow the decline in thinking ability.
• Blood circulation: some compounds in ginkgo leaf have been studied in relation to mechanisms involving blood vessels and platelets, but there is not yet enough evidence to confirm benefits for blood circulation in general.
• Antioxidants: the flavonoids in ginkgo leaf have shown antioxidant activity in laboratory studies, but clinical benefits in humans cannot yet be directly concluded.
This page is provided for information on nutritional roles only and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
ginkgo-biloba.safetyInformation:
• Ginkgo leaf extract may cause adverse effects such as headache, dizziness or digestive disturbances, and may increase the risk of bleeding when used together with anticoagulants or medicines that affect platelets.
• People with bleeding disorders, people who are about to undergo surgery, or people who take medication regularly should consult a doctor before using products containing ginkgo leaf extract.
• Use by pregnant women without medical advice is not recommended, and safety data are not yet sufficient for breastfeeding women.
keyFunctions: Contains flavonoid and terpene lactone compounds
Some of its compounds have been studied for antioxidant activity at the laboratory level
Is attracting interest in studies on mechanisms related to the nervous system and blood circulation
A plant extract with clinical research on memory and brain function

reishi-mushroom.nameTh: เห็ดหลินจือ
reishi-mushroom.shortDescription: Reishi mushroom is a mushroom of the genus Ganoderma that has long been revered in Chinese culture, earning it the nickname “the mushroom of immortality”. It is currently attracting interest in studies of its bioactive compounds, particularly beta-glucans and triterpenes.
reishi-mushroom.fullDescription:
In ancient Chinese culture, the reishi mushroom, or lingzhi, was one of the mushrooms symbolising good fortune, longevity and the wish for good health, earning it the nickname “the mushroom of immortality”, which reflects the cultural values and beliefs of the past.

Today, reishi mushroom is attracting interest in studies of its health benefits in several areas, particularly the immune response, fatigue and quality of life. The key compounds researchers are interested in include polysaccharides, particularly beta-glucans, and triterpenes, which have been studied for their biological properties and their association with cellular processes.
reishi-mushroom.howItWorks:
Reishi mushroom and how it works in the body
1. The immune response
Polysaccharides, particularly beta-glucans from reishi mushroom, have been studied for their relationship with the function of immune cells such as macrophages and certain white blood cells. Experimental results have found that these compounds may affect signalling between cells and immune response processes.
2. Processes that protect cells from oxidative stress
Reishi mushroom contains compounds that have been studied for their antioxidant properties in the laboratory, particularly triterpenes and certain phenolic compounds, which may be associated with the cellular response to oxidative stress.
3. Regulation of inflammatory processes
Cell and animal studies have found that some compounds from reishi mushroom may affect the activity of signalling molecules involved in inflammation, such as cytokines, which are part of the body's natural response processes.
4. Fatigue and quality of life
There have been some clinical studies on the use of reishi mushroom extract in people experiencing fatigue, which assessed various markers and reported results in a favourable direction.
reishi-mushroom.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of reishi mushroom
The natural reishi fruiting body is hard and woody with a bitter taste, so it is not cooked fresh like ordinary mushrooms but is processed to be consumed in various forms, as follows:
• Dried sliced reishi: fresh fruiting bodies are dried and cut into slices to be boiled in hot water and drunk as an herbal infusion.
• Reishi powder: dried fruiting bodies are ground into a fine powder, which is filled into capsules or dissolved in water to drink.
• Reishi extract: reishi goes through a decoction-extraction process with water or alcohol and is then made into a dry powder to be filled into dietary supplements in capsule or tablet form.
• Reishi spores: the spores (the brown powder released by the mushroom) go through a process that cracks their outer shell so the body can use them more easily.
reishi-mushroom.scientificEvidence:
• Polysaccharides and triterpenes from reishi mushroom have been studied at the cellular level and in laboratory animals, but these results cannot yet be used to directly confirm effectiveness in humans.
• Research on the immune system has produced varied results, and there is not yet enough clinical evidence to confirm the benefits of reishi mushroom supplements in the general population.
• Some studies on fatigue and quality of life have had limited numbers of participants or used extracts with different compositions.
This page is provided for information on nutritional roles only and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
reishi-mushroom.safetyInformation:
• Nausea, stomach discomfort, dry mouth, dizziness or an itchy rash may occur in some people.
• People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should consult a doctor before use.
• People taking immunosuppressants should consult a doctor before use.
• People taking blood-pressure-lowering medicines or medicines to control blood sugar levels should consult a doctor or pharmacist before use.
• People with liver disease should be cautious, as there have been reports of liver injury possibly associated with reishi mushroom products, although this is rare.

taurine.shortDescription: Taurine is a sulfur-containing compound found naturally in the body, particularly in the heart, brain, muscles and retina. It plays a role in maintaining cellular balance, nervous system function and the formation of bile compounds.
taurine.fullDescription:
Taurine is a compound in the amino sulfonic acid group that is found naturally in many tissues of the body. Although it is often classed as an amino acid, taurine has a chemical structure different from the amino acids used to build proteins and is not directly incorporated into protein chains.

What makes taurine of interest is its diverse roles at the cellular level, from regulating the balance of water and solutes inside cells and supporting the function of nerve tissue, to binding with bile acids to form compounds that are important for the digestion and absorption of fat.

Although taurine is a common ingredient in energy drinks, it does not stimulate the central nervous system in the same way as caffeine.
taurine.howItWorks:
Taurine and how it works in the body
1. Maintaining balance within cells
Taurine acts as one of the osmoregulators, which are involved in adjusting the balance of water and solutes inside cells, helping cells adapt to changes in their environment through physiological mechanisms.
2. Heart and nervous system function
Taurine is found in heart and nervous system tissue in biologically significant amounts and is involved in regulating intracellular calcium, cell membrane function and certain nerve signalling processes.
3. Formation of bile compounds
Taurine can bind with bile acids produced by the liver to form compounds called taurine-conjugated bile acids, which help bile acids perform their role in the digestion and absorption of fat properly.
taurine.uniqueProperties:
Food sources of taurine
• Fish and seafood, such as tuna, salmon, mussels and oysters
• Meat, such as beef, pork and lamb
• Poultry, such as chicken and turkey
• Milk and dairy products, which contain varying amounts of taurine depending on the type of product
taurine.scientificEvidence:
1. Studies on cardiovascular health
A systematic review and meta-analysis published in Nutrition Journal in 2024 evaluated clinical studies on taurine and cardiovascular markers, and found positive signals in some markers, such as blood pressure.
2. Evidence on energy and physical performance
Although taurine is a common ingredient in energy drinks, evidence on improving physical performance and brain function remains inconsistent.
3. Research on taurine and age-related changes
Taurine has attracted research interest in animal studies on the ageing process. However, a study published in the journal Science in 2025, which examined data from humans and several groups of animals, found that blood taurine levels did not consistently decline with age and are not yet suitable for use as a general marker of ageing.
This page is provided for educational purposes about taurine only and is not advice for diagnosing, preventing or treating any disease.
taurine.safetyInformation:
• Taurine obtained from ordinary food is considered part of a normal diet. When used in supplement form, the amount and the product's safety information should be considered.
• People with underlying medical conditions, especially heart disease, blood pressure disorders or kidney disease, should consult a doctor before using dietary supplements containing taurine.
• Pregnant women, breastfeeding women and children should not use high doses of taurine in supplement form without advice from a healthcare professional.
• Energy drinks should not be used as a main source of taurine, as they may contain caffeine, sugar and other ingredients that also need to be considered.
• There is not yet an official recommended daily intake of taurine for the general population, so supplement doses should not be self-determined based on clinical trial results alone.

grape-seed-extract.nameTh: เมล็ดองุ่น
grape-seed-extract.shortDescription: Grape seed extract is a source of key compounds such as proanthocyanidins, or OPCs, which have antioxidant properties and are attracting research interest in relation to blood vessel health, cell function and the skin.
grape-seed-extract.fullDescription:
Grape seeds may be a part of the grape that many people overlook, but the seeds are a source of many phytochemicals, particularly proanthocyanidins, compounds in the polyphenol group that are found naturally in many plants.

When grape seeds go through an extraction process, the resulting extract has a polyphenol composition that varies according to the raw material and production method. Oligomeric proanthocyanidins (OPCs) are one of the key compounds that attract particular interest because of their chemical properties and their association with oxidation processes.

Over the past several years, grape seed extract has been studied both in the laboratory and in human trials, particularly in relation to blood vessel markers, oxidative stress and the skin.
grape-seed-extract.howItWorks:
Grape seed and how it works in the body
Grape seed extract contains proanthocyanidins, polyphenols with a chemical structure that can take part in reactions with free radicals, which is why they are attracting interest in studies of mechanisms related to oxidative stress.
When consumed, some of the compounds are absorbed and transformed through metabolism, while proanthocyanidins with large structures may be transformed by gut microorganisms before certain metabolites are absorbed.
Researchers are also studying the association of these compounds with the mechanisms of the cells lining the blood vessel walls and the systems that regulate oxidative balance within cells.
grape-seed-extract.uniqueProperties:
Forms and consumption of grape seed
Although grape seeds are naturally found in fresh grapes, the seeds are hard and have an astringent, bitter taste, and the human digestive system cannot break down the structure of fresh seeds to make use of their key compounds. Grape seeds are therefore commonly processed industrially, as follows:
• Grape seed extract: dried grape seeds go through an extraction process and are made into a dry powder, which is filled into dietary supplements in capsule or tablet form. This is the most popular form, as it helps extract the key OPC compounds in amounts the body can use easily.
• Grape seed oil: grape seeds go through cold-press or heat extraction to obtain the oil, which is used both in cooking and as an ingredient in skincare products.
• Grape seed powder: finely ground grape seeds are used as an ingredient in drink mixes or blended into dietary supplements.
grape-seed-extract.scientificEvidence:
• Blood vessel health: a 2022 meta-analysis pooling 19 studies found changes in diastolic blood pressure and heart rate, but no significant effect on systolic blood pressure or FMD, with high heterogeneity between studies.
• Blood lipid markers: NCCIH reports that some reviews found interesting effects on LDL and triglycerides, but no firm conclusions can yet be drawn because the studies were relatively small and the extract formulas differed.
• Oxidative stress: there is laboratory-level evidence on the properties of proanthocyanidins, but these results cannot yet be used to directly confirm clinical benefits for cell protection in humans.
• Skin: a 2025 review discussed the potential of grape phytochemicals in the skin's response to UV radiation, but the study results for each compound and form of use still need to be considered separately.
This page is provided for information on composition and nutritional roles and is not advice for treating or preventing any disease.
grape-seed-extract.safetyInformation: • People taking anticoagulants or antiplatelet medicines should consult a healthcare professional before use, as information on possible interactions is still limited.
